predecessors.name: Kingdom of Cochin
predecessors.text: Fort Manuel and the Portuguese enclave at Cochin

successors.name: Republic of India
successors.text: Goa, Daman, Diu, Dadra and Nagar Haveli (Dadra and Nagar Haveli passed in 1954)

ledger.x: 1505: 'the kingdom became a protectorate in 1505' (the fort of 1503 stood on allied Cochin territory).
15 August 1505: the State of India is established with its seat at Cochin.

1510: Goa. 'Albuquerque captured Goa from the Bijapur Sultanate in 1510, and Velha Goa became the permanent settlement.' Malacca (1511) and Ormuz (1515) are also added to the State on the page but have their own dossiers.
1519: 'Quilon/Kollam (1519): became a Portuguese settlement'.
1520: Rachol.
1530: the capital moves from Cochin to Velha Goa (Old Goa), the seat until 1843 (the viceroys lived in Panjim from 1 December 1759).
1534: the Northern Province.
1535: Diu 'acquired in 1535 from the Sultan of Gujarat'.
1539: Daman. 'Sacked in 1531 and ceded in 1539'.
1558: 'a Portuguese garrison was established on Male' (the Portuguese had arrived in the Maldives in 1507).
1573: 'a popular revolt led by Muhammad Thakurufaanu al-Auzam drove the Portuguese away.'
1661: Bombay goes to England.

8 December 1661: the Dutch take Quilon ('An expedition, under Admiral Van Goens arrived in Quilon, capturing the city on the 8th of December 1661'); the page adds that the Portuguese had lost it earlier, in 1658-59.
1662-63: Cochin's Portuguese-backed Rani Gangadhara Lakshmi was captured on 5 February 1662 and handed to the Zamorin; afterwards 'the Kingdom of Cochin became a Dutch ally'.
6 or 7 January 1663: the garrison capitulates ('The forts of Cochin, Cannore and Quilon were to be handed over to the Dutch'); Cannanore fell on 15 February 1663 and Cranganore in 1662.
1739: the Marathas take the Northern Province.
1783: Nagar Haveli.
1785: 'The Portuguese bought Dadra in 1785.'
1788: the Novas Conquistas are complete.
ledger.cp: Dessais of Kudal, Sondas and Bhonslas

ledger.x: 1843: 'the capital was moved to Panjim' (Nova Goa); the viceroys had lived there since 1 December 1759.
July 1954: Dadra.
ledger.cp: United Front of Goans (Free Dadra and Nagar Haveli)

ledger.x: August 1954: Nagar Haveli.
ledger.cp: Azad Gomantak Dal (Free Dadra and Nagar Haveli)

ledger.x: 17 December 1961: 'Hostilities at Goa began at 09:45 on 17 December 1961' when Indian troops occupied Maulinguem; the main assault began at 04:00 on 18 December; Daman and Diu were attacked on 18 December.
19 December 1961: Daman surrendered at 11:00, Diu at 12:00 and the Governor General Manuel Antonio Vassalo e Silva signed the instrument of surrender for Goa at 20:30.
19 December 1961: Portuguese India ends, 'ending 451 years of Portuguese rule'.

wars.name: Portuguese conquest of Goa
wars.outcome: Albuquerque captured Goa from Bijapur in 1510 and held it.

wars.name: Dutch-Portuguese War (Malabar campaign)
wars.outcome: Quilon fell 8 December 1661, Cranganore 1662, Cochin 6/7 January 1663, Cannanore 15 February 1663: the Portuguese lost the Malabar forts and moved the garrisons to Goa.

wars.name: Maratha conquest of the Northern Province
wars.outcome: Bassein and Chaul and most of the Northern Province lost in 1739.

wars.name: Liberation of Dadra and Nagar Haveli
wars.outcome: Dadra taken 22/24 July 1954, Nagar Haveli 2 or 11 August 1954; the Portuguese lost de facto control of both.

wars.name: Portuguese wars with the Zamorin of Calicut
wars.outcome: Intermittent war from the Zamorin's 1502 demand that the Portuguese factors leave Kochi to the peace sued for in 1540 by Chinna Kutti Ali; the Zamorin page names the 1526 Siege of Calicut and gives no treaty year.

wars.name: Annexation of Goa
wars.outcome: 17-19 December 1961: Indian forces overran Goa, Daman and Diu; the Portuguese surrendered on 19 December.

certainty.note: Forts, islands and ports with no surveyed boundary; the Novas Conquistas of 1763-1788 are known only as a span.
The enclaves and Goa follow administrative talukas; the frontier with British India was fixed by treaty and survey, and Goa, Daman and Diu are the 20th-century lines.
